slides.headline: Rainy days a year, give or take
slides.body: Roseburg gets most of its 30–33 inches between October and May. A shaded roof plane may not fully dry for weeks in winter. Moss heaven.

caption:
130. That's roughly how many days a year it rains in the Umpqua Valley — and most of our 30–33 inches lands between October and May.

For your roof, that means shaded slopes can stay damp for weeks at a stretch in winter. Add tree shade and asphalt shingle texture, and you've built world-class moss habitat without even trying.

A little green fuzz now is a cheap fix. A thick mat later isn't. Free moss inspections across Douglas County — call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: What that green fuzz is actually doing up there
It lifts shingle edges
slides.body: As moss mats thicken, they pry up the edges of shingles — breaking the sealed bond that keeps wind-driven rain out.

slides.headline: It holds water like a sponge
slides.body: A moss mat stays wet for days after rain, wicking moisture into nail holes and seams and speeding up granule loss.

slides.headline: It dams the water flow
slides.body: Thick moss in valleys and along eaves pushes water sideways under shingles instead of down into your gutters.

slides.headline: A 25-year roof can fail in 15
slides.body: Under an unmanaged moss load — and moss damage is often excluded from warranty coverage as a maintenance issue.

caption:
Moss looks harmless. It isn't. Swipe for the three ways a moss mat quietly works on your shingles — lifting edges, holding water like a wet sponge, and damming the flow that's supposed to reach your gutters.

The punchline: a roof that should last 25 years can fail in 15 under an unmanaged moss load, and manufacturers usually call that a maintenance issue, not a warranty claim.

Catch it early and it's a few hundred dollars, not a new roof. Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.myth: Pressure washing is the fast way to clean a mossy roof.
slides.truth: It strips granules, drives water under shingles, voids warranties.
slides.body: If a "roof cleaner" shows up with a pressure washer, send them home.

caption:
Every year we inspect roofs that were ruined not by moss, but by the cure. A pressure washer makes a mossy roof look great for one summer — while blasting off the granules your shingles need to survive the next twenty winters.

The right way is gentle: brush the loose moss off dry, treat what remains, let Oregon's rain do the rinsing. Slower, yes. Kinder to the roof you paid five figures for, also yes.

Questions about a green roof? Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.myth: Zinc strips will kill the moss already on your roof.
slides.truth: They prevent regrowth 10–15 ft down-slope. They won't clear a mat.
slides.body: Great preventive on a clean roof. Long planes may need a second row.

caption:
Zinc strips get sold as magic. Here's the honest version: rain washing over zinc releases ions that inhibit moss growth for roughly 10–15 feet down-slope of the strip. On a clean roof, that's genuinely useful prevention — well suited to our 130-plus rain days a year.

What they won't do is clear moss that's already established. Removal first, zinc after — and long roof planes may need a second row partway down.

We install them as part of a removal-plus-prevention plan. Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: How to de-moss a roof without wrecking it
Wait for dry moss
slides.body: Late summer is ideal. Drought-stressed moss releases its grip and brushes away with far less shingle damage.

slides.headline: Brush, don't blast
slides.body: A stiff (not wire) brush, working down-slope so you never lift shingle edges. No pressure washer. Ever.

slides.headline: Treat what remains
slides.body: A zinc- or potassium-salt treatment kills the rhizoids the brush can't reach. Then Oregon's rain does the rinsing.

slides.headline: Clear the gutters after
slides.body: Dead moss keeps shedding for weeks. A follow-up gutter clean keeps that debris from starting the next problem.

caption:
The safe way to de-moss a roof, in four steps: wait for dry moss, brush down-slope, treat what's left, and clean the gutters afterward. No pressure washer anywhere in the sequence — on purpose.

One honest warning: walking a wet or mossy roof is genuinely dangerous, and steep pitches shouldn't be walked at all. If your roof is either of those, this is worth-paying-a-pro territory.

slides.headline: Why the north slope goes green first
slides.body: North- and east-facing planes see the least sun and stay damp longest. If your south slope is clean and the north is green, that's the whole story.

caption:
Drive any street in Roseburg or Myrtle Creek in February and you'll spot it: green creeping up the north slope of half the roofs on the block.

No mystery. North- and east-facing planes get the least sun, so they stay damp longest — and damp is all moss needs. Your south slope can look brand new while the north side quietly grows a lawn.

Quick habit: eyeball the north slope from the ground each winter. See fuzz? Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: Clear the runways
slides.body: Clean gutters after leaf drop and make sure the roof is shedding water cleanly going into the wet season.

slides.headline: Check from the ground
slides.body: Winter is when moss does its growing. Catching a green fuzz early beats scraping a mat later.

caption:
Moss care isn't complicated — it's just timed. Aug–Sep: remove and treat while the moss is dry and weak. Oct–Nov: gutters after leaf drop, before the rain settles in. Feb–Mar: a quick look from the ground, because winter is when moss does nearly all its growing.

slides.headline: The biggest moss fix isn't on the roof
slides.body: Overhanging limbs cast the shade moss loves and drop the litter that feeds it. Trimming them back changes the habitat — more sun, less debris, less moss.

caption:
The biggest single fix for a mossy roof usually isn't on the roof — it's the tree hanging over it.

Overhanging limbs do two things: cast the shade moss needs, and drop the needle-and-leaf litter that holds moisture and feeds growth. Trim them back and you've changed the habitat — more sun, less debris, measurably less moss.

We love our oaks and Doug-firs. Just not touching the shingles. Want a second opinion on yours? Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.truth: It's a top reason western Oregon roofs die a decade early.
slides.body: Most folks ignore it right up until the ceiling stain shows up.

caption:
"It's just moss. It's cosmetic." We hear it weekly — usually about two winters before the ceiling stain.

Moss is one of the most common reasons western Oregon roofs die a decade early. It pries up shingle edges, holds water against the deck, and blocks drainage — none of which shows from the driveway until it's expensive.

The good news: caught early, it's neither hard nor costly to fix. Free inspections across Douglas County. Call or text (541) 670-5005.

slides.headline: Black grit in your gutters? That's your roof's armor.
slides.body: Shingle granules protect against UV and rain. Some loss is normal — heavy grit on an older roof or below a mossy slope means fast aging.

caption:
Five-minute homeowner check: run a hand through your gutter after a rain. Black, sandy grit? Those are shingle granules — your roof's UV armor, washing away.

Some loss is normal, especially on a newer roof. But heavy grit on an older roof, or below a mossy slope, means the shingles are aging fast right where it counts.

Not sure how much is too much? Send us a photo — call or text (541) 670-5005 and we'll give you a straight answer.

slides.headline: Can you de-moss your own roof? Sometimes, yes.
slides.body: Low pitch, dry day, soft brush, down-slope strokes — doable. Steep, wet, or two stories up? That's what we're for. Mossy roofs are dangerous to walk.

caption:
Honest answer to a common question: yes, some homeowners can de-moss their own roof. Low pitch, single story, dry day, soft brush, down-slope strokes — that's a reasonable Saturday.

Steep pitch, two stories, wet shingles, or an established mat? Please don't. We'd rather quote you $250–600 than have you meet the ground.

Either way: skip the pressure washer, and treat after you brush. Questions? Call or text (541) 670-5005 — free advice is free.

slides.headline: A valley, prepped the boring way

caption:
From a real job: a valley, prepped and ready. Valleys are where two roof planes dump their water into one channel — the hardest-working real estate on any roof, and the first place shortcuts show up as leaks.

So we prep them the boring way: clean deck, proper underlayment, everything sealed before a single shingle goes down. Boring is the point.
